stem: An intrusion is discovered after fourteen months. Nothing was encrypted, no ransom was demanded, no systems were disrupted, and the only activity found was steady copying of engineering design documents. What was the motivation?

options.text: Espionage
options.why: Long dwell time, no damage, and theft of intellectual property. The absence of disruption is the signal: the attacker needed access to continue, so breaking anything would have been counterproductive.

options.text: Service disruption
options.why: Nothing was disrupted. Fourteen months of quiet is the opposite of this motive.

options.text: Financial gain
options.why: Possible downstream if the designs are sold, and the stem gives no demand, no fraud and no monetisation. The direct objective described is the information.

options.text: Disruption and chaos
options.why: That motive produces visible disorder. This attacker worked hard to remain invisible.

stem: Attackers copy a customer database, then encrypt the production systems and demand payment both to restore access and to not publish the stolen records. Which motivation best describes the second demand?

options.text: Blackmail, used as a lever to secure financial gain
options.why: Double extortion: the threat to publish is leverage. The underlying motive is money, and the name for that threat is blackmail.

options.text: Espionage, since data was exfiltrated
options.why: Espionage keeps the theft secret because the value is in continued access. Announcing it destroys that value.

options.text: Service disruption
options.why: That describes the encryption half. The question asks about the threat to publish.

options.text: Philosophical or political beliefs
options.why: No cause or message is involved; the demand is payment.

stem: During an armed conflict, a neighbouring state's power distribution control systems are hit with destructive malware that wipes controllers. No ransom is demanded and nothing is stolen. Which motivation applies?

options.text: War, pursued through service disruption of critical infrastructure
options.why: War is a motivation in its own right. The mechanism is service disruption, and the context of state conflict and critical national infrastructure is what distinguishes it.

options.text: Disruption and chaos for its own sake
options.why: That motive has no strategic beneficiary. Here the conflict supplies an obvious one.

options.text: Financial gain
options.why: No demand and no monetisation. Wiping controllers destroys value rather than extracting it.

options.text: Revenge
options.why: Revenge targets a specific party over a personal grievance, not a state's infrastructure during a conflict.

stem: A researcher discovers an authentication bypass in a public service, does not use it to access any data, and reports it privately to the vendor. Which motivation is this?

options.text: Ethical
options.why: Ethical is a motivation in its own right. The defining behaviour is reporting the flaw rather than exploiting it, whether or not permission was held in advance.

options.text: Philosophical or political beliefs
options.why: That motive seeks to make a public point, typically through defacement or a leak.

options.text: Financial gain, since a bounty may be paid
options.why: A bounty may follow and the stem describes a private report with no demand. Motivation is judged on the behaviour described.

options.text: Revenge
options.why: No grievance or target relationship is described.

stem: Which attribute distinguishes an insider threat from an external attacker who has stolen valid credentials?

options.text: The insider is legitimately inside the organisation and holds authorised access as part of their role
options.why: Internal versus external is about the actor's relationship to the organisation, not about whether they currently hold working credentials. An outsider with stolen credentials remains external.

options.text: The insider always acts maliciously
options.why: Insider threat includes negligence and coercion. Intent is a separate axis from position.

options.text: The insider has greater technical sophistication
options.why: Sophistication is its own attribute and varies independently. Many insiders have none.

options.text: The insider operates from inside the network perimeter
options.why: Insiders often work remotely, and attackers routinely reach inside the perimeter. Location is not the distinction.

stem: An intrusion uses two previously unknown vulnerabilities, custom tooling that matches no public sample, and maintains access for months without detection. Which two actor attributes does this most strongly evidence?

options.text: High resources and funding, and high sophistication or capability
options.why: Zero-days are expensive to acquire or develop, and custom tooling with long undetected persistence requires sustained skilled effort. These are the two attributes that point to a highly capable actor.

options.text: Internal position and high sophistication
options.why: Nothing indicates the actor is inside the organisation.

options.text: Low resources and high motivation
options.why: Zero-days and bespoke tooling are the signature of significant funding, not of determination on a budget.

options.text: High resources and a financial motivation
options.why: Resources are evidenced; motivation is not stated. The question asks about attributes, and inferring a motive here would be a guess.

stem: An administrator is told they will be made redundant in a month. Two weeks later a scheduled task is discovered that will delete backups after their final day. What motivation and actor type does this represent?

options.text: An insider threat motivated by revenge
options.why: A named grievance against a specific organisation, acted on by someone with authorised access. Both the actor type and the motivation are given directly by the scenario.

options.text: An insider threat motivated by financial gain
options.why: Nothing is being stolen or sold. Destroying backups makes no money.

options.text: An external attacker motivated by service disruption
options.why: The actor is a current employee with legitimate access.

options.text: Shadow IT, since the task was created outside change control
options.why: Shadow IT is unsanctioned technology adopted to get work done, not deliberate sabotage.

stem: A group defaces several unrelated small business websites with crude graphics, makes no demand, steals nothing, and publicises the results for attention. Which motivation fits best?

options.text: Disruption or chaos, including notoriety
options.why: No beneficiary, no demand, no coherent cause, and unrelated targets chosen for availability rather than meaning. Attention is the return.

options.text: Philosophical or political beliefs
options.why: That motive carries a message and chooses targets connected to the cause. Unrelated small businesses and crude graphics indicate neither.

options.text: Financial gain
options.why: Nothing is monetised and no payment is demanded.

options.text: Service disruption as a strategic objective
options.why: Strategic disruption targets something whose outage matters to a specific party. These targets were interchangeable.

stem: An intrusion used two previously unknown vulnerabilities, maintained access for eleven months without detection, and targeted defence contract documents. Which threat actor is most likely?

options.text: A nation-state actor
options.why: Zero-day capability, very long dwell time and an espionage target together indicate resources and patience that only a state sponsored actor typically has.

options.text: Organised crime
options.why: Criminal groups are well funded and motivated by money. Eleven quiet months on defence documents with no monetisation does not fit.

options.text: A hacktivist
options.why: Hacktivists have limited resources and want visibility. Staying hidden for eleven months defeats their purpose.

options.text: An unskilled attacker
options.why: Unskilled attackers use off the shelf tools. They do not develop zero-days.

stem: A group defaces a company's website with political slogans on the day of a controversial government vote, and publicises it widely. Which actor and motivation?

options.text: A hacktivist motivated by political beliefs
options.why: Visible defacement timed to a political event, with publicity as the goal, is the hacktivist signature.

options.text: Organised crime motivated by financial gain
options.why: No money is being extracted, and publicity is the opposite of what a criminal group wants.

options.text: A nation-state motivated by espionage
options.why: Espionage requires staying hidden. Defacement announces the intrusion immediately.

options.text: An insider threat motivated by revenge
options.why: Nothing indicates the attacker had legitimate access, and the motivation is stated as political.

stem: A marketing team signs up for an unapproved cloud file sharing service and moves campaign material into it, without malicious intent. How is this classified?

options.text: Shadow IT
options.why: Technology adopted outside the approved process by employees trying to do their jobs. It creates real risk without any malicious intent.

options.text: A malicious insider threat
options.why: The scenario states there is no malicious intent. Treating convenience as sabotage misidentifies both the actor and the fix.

options.text: An unskilled attacker
options.why: Nobody is attacking. Employees adopted a tool.

options.text: A supply chain compromise
options.why: No vendor relationship was abused. The organisation simply has no relationship with this vendor at all.

stem: A departing engineer downloads the full customer database on their last afternoon, going directly to the one share containing it. Which characteristic most identifies this actor type?

options.text: Legitimate access and knowledge of exactly where the valuable data sits
options.why: An insider does not need to intrude or discover anything. That is precisely what makes insiders so difficult to detect with perimeter controls.

options.text: Advanced tooling and zero-day capability
options.why: That describes a nation-state. An insider needs no exploit because they already have credentials.

options.text: Large financial backing
options.why: Resources describe organised crime and nation-states. An insider's advantage is access, not funding.

options.text: A desire for public attention
options.why: That is hacktivist behaviour. This actor is acting quietly on their way out.

stem: A web server is defaced shortly after a public exploit for a three-year-old flaw is published. Logs show the same exploit string tried against hundreds of unrelated addresses, with no sign of follow-up access. Which actor and defensive conclusion best fit?

options.text: A nation-state actor, so the organization should assume an unknown vulnerability and unlimited resources
options.why: Nothing suggests an unknown flaw or a focused target. A public exploit sprayed at many addresses is the opposite of the patient, targeted work of a state.

options.text: An unskilled attacker using public tools, so patching known flaws would have stopped it
options.why: Low capability, low resources and an opportunistic, untargeted approach point here. These actors depend on known weaknesses that routine patching removes.

options.text: Organized crime, so the organization should expect a ransom demand next
options.why: Crime groups are profit driven. A defacement with no demand and no follow-up shows no sign of a monetary goal.

options.text: A hacktivist, because a defacement always carries a political message
options.why: Defacement alone does not show a cause. Without a message tied to a belief, the better explanation is opportunism with ready-made tools.

stem: An intrusion shows access bought from a broker of stolen credentials, widely available commodity tools, and a ransom negotiation handled in a staffed chat service. The group left within a day of payment and has hit forty unrelated companies this quarter. Which statement best describes the actor?

options.text: Organized crime: well funded and organized, using commodity tools, motivated by financial gain
options.why: A division of labour, repeated unrelated victims, and a payment-driven exit are the signs of a business. It is organized without being highly sophisticated.

options.text: A nation-state actor, because the operation is well resourced and well organized
options.why: Resources and organization are shared by several actors. Motivation separates them: a state pursues strategic goals and persistence, not a quick exit after payment.

options.text: A hacktivist group, because its activity is publicized and coordinated
options.why: Hacktivists act for a cause and rarely seek payment. Forty unrelated victims and a negotiated price point to profit.

options.text: An insider threat, because the attackers used valid credentials
options.why: Valid credentials bought from a broker do not make the actor an insider. The attacker remained external throughout.

stem: A product team, frustrated by procurement delays, builds a cloud test environment on a personal credit card. It holds copies of production data and is reachable from the internet with default credentials. An external attacker later finds it. Which description of the original exposure is best?

options.text: An insider threat motivated by revenge against the procurement team
options.why: No malice is described. The team wanted to work faster. Revenge would need a grievance expressed as damage.

options.text: Shadow IT: unmanaged systems built by well-meaning staff, outside the organization's security visibility
options.why: Shadow IT is the use of systems the organization does not know about or control. The risk comes from the lack of oversight, not from hostile intent.

options.text: A hacktivist, because the attacker targeted a company with a public profile
options.why: The attacker is not described as having a cause. The exposure existed because of an unmanaged system, whoever found it.

options.text: An unskilled attacker, because default credentials were used to get in
options.why: The attacker may or may not be skilled. The weakness that made the intrusion easy was created internally by the team.

stem: A group breaks into an energy company, copies internal emails that show lobbying against emissions rules, and gives them to journalists. It demands nothing, sells nothing and says publicly that it acted to expose the company. Which actor and motivation fit best?

options.text: A hacktivist, driven by political beliefs, exposing the company rather than profiting
options.why: The target was chosen for what it represents, the data was released and not sold, and the stated aim is a cause. That matches a hacktivist.

options.text: A nation-state actor engaged in espionage on the energy sector
options.why: Espionage means taking information quietly for the benefit of the actor. Handing it to journalists is the opposite.

options.text: An ethical hacker, because the group acted in the public interest
options.why: Ethical describes authorized testing and responsible disclosure. A group that breaks in without permission and publishes is not that.

options.text: Organized crime using blackmail, because the emails could embarrass the company
options.why: Blackmail needs a demand with a way to avoid disclosure. Here the data was released and nothing was asked for.

stem: An investigator is asked whether an intrusion is more likely a nation-state actor than a financially motivated criminal group. Which TWO observations most strongly support the nation-state view? (Choose two.)

options.text: The attackers kept access for fourteen months and made no attempt to profit from it
options.why: Long, quiet persistence with no monetization points to a goal other than money, such as collecting intelligence.

options.text: A demand for payment in cryptocurrency was sent on the day access was discovered
options.why: A payment demand is the clearest sign of a profit motive, which points away from a state.

options.text: The stolen documents all concerned a ministry's position in an upcoming trade negotiation
options.why: Targeting by strategic value, not by ability to pay, is characteristic of a state serving its own interests.

options.text: The ransomware used was a publicly sold builder that other groups also use
options.why: Commodity tooling is common among criminals and suggests lower investment. It does not point to a state.

options.text: The stolen data was posted on a leak site with a countdown timer
options.why: A countdown timer is a pressure tactic to extract payment, typical of criminals.

stem: Months before a regional conflict begins, investigators find a quiet intrusion in the control systems of another country's regional power and telecom networks. Nothing was copied and nothing was changed. The attackers left tools in place and tested that they could reach the controllers. Which motivation best describes this activity?

options.text: Espionage, because the attackers remained undetected for months inside a strategic network
options.why: Espionage gathers information. Here nothing was taken and the access was aimed at the controllers, not at documents.

options.text: Financial gain, because attackers who prepare access are usually selling it later
options.why: Nothing points to sale. The target and the timing before a conflict show a strategic aim.

options.text: Philosophical or political beliefs, because the target is a government-linked network
options.why: That motivation is a cause expressed publicly. Quiet preparation of a means to disrupt is not.

options.text: War: pre-positioning to be able to disrupt critical infrastructure when conflict starts
options.why: No data was taken, and the access went to the systems that run power and communications. This is preparation to disrupt as a weapon of war.

stem: Over six months, thirty unrelated companies report that their customer databases were copied. No systems were encrypted and no demand was made. The same records then appear for sale on an underground marketplace. Which motivation best describes the attackers?

options.text: Espionage, because the data was taken quietly and kept for a long time
options.why: Espionage serves a state or a rival seeking strategic information. Selling records to anyone who pays is commerce.

options.text: Revenge against the companies, because customer data was exposed
options.why: Nothing links the thirty victims by a grievance. Unrelated targets and a marketplace listing point to profit.

options.text: Disruption or chaos, because the breach harmed many organizations
options.why: Harm was a side effect. Disruption would show in damaged systems or publicity, and here the attackers took care to stay quiet and sell.

options.text: Financial gain through data theft, typical of organized crime selling stolen records
options.why: Theft of data that has market value and is then sold shows a profit motive. No ransom is needed when the data itself is the product.

stem: A security team is building a threat model for a regional hospital. Which TWO statements are the most defensible? (Choose two.)

options.text: A financially motivated criminal group deploying ransomware is the most likely external actor
options.why: Likelihood follows motivation and opportunity. A hospital has urgency and data, which is what a profit-driven group looks for.

options.text: A nation-state actor is the most likely external actor, because hospitals hold sensitive personal data
options.why: Sensitive data attracts criminals as much as anyone. A state is likely only when the hospital serves a strategic purpose, such as research or military care.

options.text: Insiders with legitimate access belong in the model alongside external actors
options.why: Insiders already hold access and know where the data sits, so they need controls and monitoring even when no malice is assumed.

options.text: Hacktivists are the primary concern, because hospitals are controversial
options.why: A cause is what drives a hacktivist. A hospital without a political profile is rarely chosen for that reason.

options.text: Unskilled attackers can be left out, because they cannot cause serious harm
options.why: They use public tools against known weaknesses, so exposed and unpatched systems are still at risk of them.

stem: An employee with access to the executive mailboxes copies a private thread and tells the chief executive that it will be sent to the board unless the employee is given a senior role and the project they have been asking for. There is no cash demand and no known grievance. Which motivation best describes this?

options.text: Revenge, because the employee is using damaging material against a superior
options.why: Revenge is about punishing someone for a wrong. Here the employee wants something in return and offers silence, and nothing suggests a grievance.

options.text: Blackmail by an insider: a threat to disclose is used to force a benefit
options.why: Blackmail is a demand backed by a threat of disclosure, and the demand need not be money. The legitimate access marks the actor as internal.

options.text: Data exfiltration, because the employee copied data from a mailbox
options.why: Copying is the means. The motivation is the benefit the employee wants to force, which is why the data is held back.

options.text: Disruption or chaos, because the employee is creating a crisis for management
options.why: A crisis is not the aim. The employee wants the crisis avoided in exchange for a benefit.

stem: During a conflict, a loosely organized group of volunteers with no known state link announces on social media that it will flood the websites of banks in one country. It uses freely available tools, steals nothing and says it acts to support one side. Which actor is the best fit?

options.text: A nation-state actor, because the activity is timed with a military conflict
options.why: Timing alone does not show state control. Volunteers, public announcements and free tools are signs of a group acting by belief.

options.text: An unskilled attacker, because the tools are freely available
options.why: The tools are basic, but the actor has a stated cause and a campaign. Capability is only one attribute, and motivation decides the category.

options.text: A hacktivist group, using service disruption for political beliefs
options.why: Volunteers who act for a cause, announce what they do and take nothing fit a hacktivist. Flooding sites is a typical low-skill method.

options.text: Organized crime, because the attack is coordinated across many targets
options.why: Coordination alone is not profit. There is no payment, no theft and no ransom, so the motive is not financial.

stem: A report says a well-funded group buys zero-day exploits from brokers and rents global infrastructure, but its only goal is extorting payment from companies. A colleague concludes that anything this well funded must be a nation-state. What is the flaw in the conclusion?

options.text: There is none: funding level is the best way to tell a nation-state from other actors
options.why: Funding is one attribute, and several actors can have a lot of it. It cannot separate one from another on its own.

options.text: Capability is an attribute, but motivation decides the type: extortion for payment is organized crime
options.why: Funding describes what an actor can do. The goal, here profit by extortion, describes who they are likely to be.

options.text: Organized crime cannot buy zero-day exploits, so the report must be wrong
options.why: Criminal groups can and do buy them. High capability is not exclusive to states.

options.text: Only an insider can be both well funded and motivated by payment
options.why: Insiders are defined by their access, not by funding. Nothing in the report suggests anyone inside the victim.

stem: A company's first report on an intrusion says it was a nation-state attack, because the malware used techniques that appeared in leaked government tooling. A later review finds a ransom note, a payment wallet and a criminal group using the leaked tools. What is the right lesson?

options.text: Sophistication of tools identifies the actor, so the first report was right and the criminals must have been state-sponsored
options.why: Leaked tools can be used by anyone. The review found a payment demand and a criminal group, so the first conclusion was not supported.

options.text: Capability should never be considered when identifying an actor, because every actor has access to the same tools
options.why: Capability is a useful attribute. It is just not enough alone, and it should be read together with motive and behavior.

options.text: Tooling alone does not identify an actor: weigh motivation and behavior, such as a ransom demand, with capability
options.why: Attribution by capability is weak when tools circulate. The ransom note and wallet showed a profit motive that the tooling did not.

options.text: Ransom notes always indicate a hacktivist, so the later review was wrong to name a criminal group
options.why: Hacktivists act for a cause and do not normally demand payment. A wallet and a demand point to profit.
